lessons.title: Work, study and daily tasks
lessons.description: Talk about work, study and common tasks.

vocabulary.example: I work in an office.
My colleague is helpful.
The meeting starts at nine.
I study English every day.
This is my first task.

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: Where do you work?
B: I work in an office.
A: Do you have a meeting today?
B: Yes, at nine o’clock.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Use “I work” for a routine. Use “I am working” for an activity happening now.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: With I, use the base verb: I work.

quiz.question: What is a colleague?
quiz.explanation: A colleague is someone you work with.

lessons.title: Talking about last weekend
lessons.description: Describe completed activities using common past-simple verbs.

vocabulary.example: We visited our friends on Friday.
She bought a new book.
They went to the market.
I stayed at home.
We enjoyed the trip.

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: What did you do last weekend?
B: I visited my family and went to the market.
A: Did you enjoy it?
B: Yes, I did.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: In past questions, use did + the base verb: Did you go?

quiz.question: Choose the correct question.
quiz.explanation: After did, use the base form go.

quiz.question: Past form of buy:
quiz.explanation: Buy is irregular; its past form is bought.

vocabulary.example: It is sunny today.
It is rainy this morning.
Take your jacket.
These shoes are comfortable.
It is cold outside.

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: What is the weather like?
B: It is cold and rainy.
A: Take your jacket.
B: Good idea, thank you.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Use “It is…” to describe weather: It is sunny. It is cold.

quiz.question: Which word describes wet weather?
quiz.explanation: Rainy means that rain is falling or likely.

quiz.question: Complete: It ___ cold today.
quiz.explanation: Use “it is” to describe the weather.

lessons.title: Making appointments
lessons.description: Arrange a meeting and respond politely.

vocabulary.example: Are you available tomorrow?
I have an appointment at ten.
Can we reschedule the meeting?
Please confirm the time.
Is three o’clock convenient?

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: Are you available on Tuesday?
B: I am available after two.
A: Shall we meet at three?
B: That is convenient.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: “Could we…?” and “Would … be convenient?” are polite ways to arrange a meeting.

quiz.question: Choose a polite suggestion.
quiz.explanation: Could we…? is a polite suggestion.

quiz.question: What does reschedule mean?
quiz.explanation: To reschedule is to arrange a new date or time.

lessons.title: Health problems and advice
lessons.description: Describe common symptoms and understand everyday advice.

vocabulary.example: I have a headache.
He has a fever.
You should get some rest.
Take the medicine as directed.
A cough can be a symptom.

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: What is wrong?
B: I have a headache.
A: You should rest.
B: Thank you.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Use should + base verb to give advice: You should rest.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence.
quiz.explanation: Use should followed by the base verb.

quiz.question: A headache is a…
quiz.explanation: A headache is a symptom.

lessons.title: Giving opinions and reasons
lessons.description: Express an opinion, support it with reasons and disagree politely.

vocabulary.example: In my view, practice is essential.
The plan is useful; however, it is expensive.
The road was closed; therefore, we arrived late.
Although it was difficult, we finished.
The evidence supports this view.

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: In my view, online lessons save time.
B: I agree to some extent. However, classroom practice is also useful.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Use however to introduce contrast and therefore to introduce a result.

quiz.question: Which connector introduces a result?
quiz.explanation: Therefore introduces a consequence or result.

quiz.question: Choose a polite disagreement.
options: I see your point, but I have a different view.
quiz.explanation: This phrase acknowledges the other person before disagreeing.

lessons.title: Transport and travel
lessons.description: Ask about transport, tickets and travel times.

vocabulary.example: The bus stop is near the bank.
I need one ticket, please.
The train station is downtown.
The train leaves from platform two.
Can I have a return ticket?

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: Excuse me, where is the bus station?
B: Go straight and turn left.
A: Thank you. How much is a ticket?
B: It is five pounds.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Use “Where is…?” to ask for a place and “How much is…?” to ask for a price.

quiz.question: Which phrase asks about price?
quiz.explanation: How much is…? asks about cost.

quiz.question: A platform is usually found at a…
quiz.explanation: Passengers wait on a platform at a station.

lessons.title: Asking for help politely
lessons.description: Use simple polite expressions when asking for help.

vocabulary.example: Could you help me, please?
Please speak slowly.
Could you repeat that?
I do not understand this word.
Thank you for your help.

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: Could you help me, please?
B: Of course. What do you need?
A: Could you repeat that slowly?
B: Certainly.

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: Could you…? is a polite way to make a request. Add please to sound friendly.

quiz.question: Choose a polite request.
quiz.explanation: Could you… please? is polite and natural.

quiz.question: What does repeat mean?
quiz.explanation: Repeat means to say or do something again.

lessons.title: Ordering food at a restaurant
lessons.description: Order food, ask about ingredients and request the bill.

vocabulary.example: Could I see the menu, please?
I would like to order soup.
What are the ingredients?
Can I have salad as a side dish?
Could we have the bill, please?

sections.heading: Useful dialogue
sections.body:
A: Are you ready to order?
B: Yes, I would like chicken and rice.
A: Would you like a drink?
B: Water, please. And could we have the bill later?

sections.heading: Language tip
sections.body: “I would like…” is a polite way to order. Use “Could we have…?” to request something.

quiz.question: Which phrase politely asks for the bill?
options: Could we have the bill, please?
quiz.explanation: Could we have… please? is polite and clear.

quiz.question: Ingredients are…
options: The items used to make food
quiz.explanation: Ingredients are the foods or substances used in a dish.

lessons.title: Writing a clear professional email
lessons.description: Write concise professional emails with a clear request and next step.

vocabulary.example: I am writing regarding your request.
Please find the attached document.
Could you clarify the deadline?
Thank you in advance for your help.
Kind regards, Alex.

sections.heading: Email example
sections.body:
Dear Ms Lee,
I am writing regarding the meeting scheduled for Thursday. Could you please clarify the start time? I have attached the updated agenda.
Kind regards,
Alex

sections.heading: Writing tip
sections.body: Use a meaningful subject, put the request near the beginning, and explain the next step. Keep each paragraph focused on one idea.

quiz.question: Which phrase refers to a document sent with an email?
quiz.explanation: Attached describes a file included with the message.

quiz.question: What makes a professional email clearer?
options: A clear request and next step
quiz.explanation: A clear purpose and next step help the reader respond.

lessons.title: Evaluating evidence and arguments
lessons.description: Compare claims with evidence and express qualified conclusions.
objectives: Distinguish a claim from supporting evidence
Use cautious language when evaluating information

vocabulary.example: The evidence supports the main conclusion.
We need a reliable source before making a claim.
The argument depends on an assumption.
The sample was small; nevertheless, the result is useful.
There is substantial evidence for the proposal.

sections.heading: Reading
sections.body: A strong argument states a clear claim and supports it with relevant evidence. A reliable source explains where its information came from. If evidence is incomplete, a careful writer acknowledges the limitation rather than presenting an assumption as a fact.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Use although, whereas, nevertheless and therefore to show contrast and consequence. Phrases such as “the evidence suggests” are more cautious than “this proves” when certainty is limited.

quiz.question: Which word introduces a contrast with the previous statement?
quiz.explanation: Nevertheless signals contrast or an unexpected result.

quiz.question: A reliable source is one that is…
quiz.explanation: Reliable means likely to be accurate or trustworthy.

quiz.question: Which sentence is appropriately cautious?
options: The findings suggest a possible link.
quiz.explanation: Suggests a possible link communicates a qualified conclusion.

lessons.title: Nuanced discussion and synthesis
lessons.description: Synthesize different viewpoints and qualify complex claims.
objectives: Qualify a conclusion without losing clarity

vocabulary.example: The first approach is inexpensive; conversely, it takes longer.
Whereas demand increased, supply remained stable.
The proposal is, to some extent, effective.
Independent data corroborate the initial findings.
One implication is that training must change.

sections.heading: Model paragraph
sections.body: Although the proposal may reduce short-term costs, its long-term implications remain uncertain. Independent data corroborate some of the expected benefits, whereas other findings point to implementation risks. To some extent, the outcome will depend on how consistently the policy is applied.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Synthesis connects ideas rather than listing them. Use concessive clauses to acknowledge a limitation, contrast markers to compare evidence, and qualified expressions to avoid overstating a conclusion.

quiz.question: What does corroborate mean?
quiz.explanation: Corroborate means confirm or support with additional evidence.

quiz.question: Which phrase explicitly limits the strength of a claim?
quiz.explanation: To some extent indicates a qualified or partial claim.

quiz.question: A synthesis should…
options: Connect and compare ideas from different sources
quiz.explanation: Synthesis explains relationships between ideas and sources.

lessons.title: Precision, register and rhetorical control
lessons.description: Choose precise wording and adapt register for complex professional communication.
objectives: Adapt register to audience and purpose
Revise a complex statement for precision

vocabulary.example: The conclusion is valid insofar as the data are accurate.
The report offers a tentative explanation.
The salient issue is the lack of comparable data.
The results underscore the need for careful review.
A conspicuous omission weakens the report.

sections.heading: Editing exercise
sections.body: Less precise: “The report says the plan is bad.” More precise: “The report identifies substantial implementation risks and offers a tentative explanation for the projected shortfall.” The revision distinguishes the source's finding from the writer's own judgment.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: At advanced levels, accuracy includes register, implication and degree of certainty. Use “insofar as” to state a limit, “salient” to identify what matters most, and “tentative” when a conclusion remains provisional.

quiz.question: Which adjective identifies the most important point?
quiz.explanation: Salient means most noticeable or important in a particular context.

quiz.question: A tentative conclusion is…
quiz.explanation: Tentative indicates caution or incomplete certainty.

quiz.question: Why revise “the plan is bad” in a professional report?
options: To state specific risks and the basis for the assessment
To make the claim less clear
quiz.explanation: Precise wording identifies the nature and basis of an evaluation.

lessons.title: Negotiating practical solutions
lessons.description: Negotiate options politely and explain trade-offs.

vocabulary.example: There is a trade-off between speed and cost.
The revised schedule is feasible.
Both teams accepted a compromise.
Could you clarify the delivery date?
We have tentatively agreed to meet on Friday.

sections.heading: Dialogue
sections.body: A: The deadline may be difficult to meet. B: Could we deliver the first stage on Friday and the rest next week? A: That seems feasible. Let us clarify responsibilities.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Use could we…? to suggest options politely. A trade-off describes what is gained and sacrificed. Tentatively signals that an arrangement is not final.

quiz.question: A trade-off is…
options: A balance between competing benefits and costs
quiz.explanation: A trade-off involves accepting a limitation in exchange for another benefit.

quiz.question: Which phrase politely suggests an option?
options: Could we deliver the first stage on Friday?
quiz.explanation: Could we…? is a collaborative way to suggest an option.

quiz.question: A tentative agreement is…
quiz.explanation: Tentative means provisional or subject to confirmation.

lessons.title: Presenting a complex issue clearly
lessons.description: Structure a concise presentation of a complex issue.

vocabulary.example: The main counterargument concerns cost.
On balance, the second option is preferable.
Implementation will require staff training.
My recommendation is to run a pilot.
First, I will signpost the main issues.

sections.heading: Presentation extract
sections.body: The proposal could reduce delays. The main counterargument concerns implementation costs. On balance, the evidence supports a limited pilot rather than a full launch. I recommend a three-month trial with clear measures of success.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Signposting phrases guide listeners. Present a counterargument fairly before responding to it, and distinguish reported evidence from your own recommendation.

quiz.question: A counterargument…
options: Presents a reason against a position
quiz.explanation: A counterargument challenges or qualifies the main position.

quiz.question: Which phrase signals a conclusion after weighing factors?
quiz.explanation: On balance introduces a conclusion after considering different factors.

quiz.question: A recommendation should be…
options: Distinguished from the evidence supporting it
Presented as a proven fact without support
quiz.explanation: Professional communication separates findings from proposed actions.

lessons.title: Editing for precision and tone
lessons.description: Revise professional prose for precision, nuance and register.
objectives: Replace vague claims with specific descriptions

vocabulary.example: The instruction is ambiguous about who must respond.
The report does not substantiate that conclusion.
The response should be proportionate to the risk.
The process should not be unduly burdensome.
State precisely which figures require revision.

sections.heading: Editing example
sections.body: Vague: “The process is bad.” Revised: “The current process creates avoidable delays and places a disproportionate administrative burden on small teams.” The revision identifies the problem without an unsupported absolute judgment.

sections.heading: Language focus
sections.body: Choose verbs that match the evidence: indicate, suggest, demonstrate or substantiate. Avoid absolute wording unless the evidence warrants it.

quiz.question: Substantiate means…
quiz.explanation: To substantiate is to support an assertion with evidence.

quiz.question: An ambiguous instruction…
options: Can be understood in more than one way
quiz.explanation: Ambiguity arises when wording allows multiple interpretations.

quiz.question: Why avoid absolute claims without strong evidence?
options: They may overstate what the evidence establishes
quiz.explanation: The strength of a claim should match the strength of its evidence.
